title: Notebook07
text:
Setup
Run all of the following before starting the notebook.


View code
! wget -q -nc https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/funs.py




View code
import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"




View code
storm = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/storms.csv")




Questions
We are staying with the North Atlantic storms from last time. Each row is one observation of one storm at one moment, taken every six hours, with the position of the storm’s center (lon, lat), its wind speed in knots (wind), its Saffir-Simpson category, a two-letter status code, and the name and year that together identify which storm it belongs to. The column doy gives the day of the year.
Last time we had only one geometry and one color of point. This notebook adds the rest of the layer: the aesthetics that carry extra columns into the plot, and the geometries other than points.
Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it to a variable.

Plot the tracks of the 2005 season again, longitude against latitude, but map the name column to the color aesthetic so that each storm gets its own color. Remember that every aesthetic other than x and y goes inside a second call to aes(), placed inside the geometry.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.name))
)









Last week these 688 points were an anonymous tangle. One aesthetic separates them into 21 storms, and the legend tells you which is which.

A color can also be set to a fixed value rather than mapped to a column, and the same is true of alpha, which controls how transparent each point is. Recall that the very first plot of the last notebook, all 25,112 observations at once, came out as a solid black mass. Draw it again with alpha fixed at 0.05.



View code
(
    storm
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.05)
)









Twenty points must now stack up before the ink is fully black, so the darkness of a region tells you how many storms have passed through it. The corridor from the Caribbean through the Gulf is the darkest part of the plot. You can also pick out the storms that form off the coast of Africa on the right and run west across the open ocean, and the pale fan at the top where the survivors curve away to the northeast and die in the cold water.
Note the syntax: alpha=0.05 sits inside geom_point() but outside aes(). A value inside aes() is a column name; a value outside it is a constant. This is the single most common mistake people make with this package.

Map the color aesthetic to category instead, for the 2005 season. The legend comes out looking quite different from the one in question 1. Why?



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.category))
)









Answer: The legend is a continuous color bar rather than a list of labeled swatches, because category has type i64. The package looks at the type of the column, sees a number, and assumes the values fall on a scale where 4 lies between 3 and 5. It cannot know that there are only seven possible values and that they are really labels. With name, a str, it had no choice but to treat each value as a separate group.

The fix is a cast, from Chapter 3. Convert category to a string inside .with_columns() before you plot it, and compare the result with question 3.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .with_columns(category = c.category.cast(pl.String))
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(aes(color=c.category))
)









Seven discrete colors, one legend entry each. It is easier now to see that the strongest parts of a storm happen in short bursts: most of every track is dark purple, and the two or three days at category 4 or 5 are a small bright stretch in the middle. The type of a column is not just a storage detail. It decides what the plot looks like.

Now put names on the map. We want one row per storm, positioned at the moment that storm was at its strongest. Sort the 2005 season by wind, largest first, and then keep the first row for each name. Save the result as peak, since we will use it several times, and print it.



View code
peak = (
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .sort(c.wind, descending=True)
    .unique(subset=["name"], keep="first", maintain_order=True)
    .select(c.name, c.lon, c.lat, c.wind, c.status)
)

The maintain_order=True argument is what makes this work. Without it Polars is free to return the rows of a .unique() in whatever order is fastest, and “keep the first row” would stop meaning “keep the strongest”.
Use the text geometry to label each storm’s peak on the map. The text geometry needs a third aesthetic, label, in addition to x and y.


View code
(
    peak
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_text(aes(label=c.name))
)










The labels tell you which storm is which but not exactly where it was, since a word has no obvious center. Add a point geometry underneath the text, then shrink the labels and nudge them upward so they sit above their points.



View code
(
    peak
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
    .geom_text(aes(label=c.name), size=8, nudge_y=1.0)
)









The 2005 season is famous for having exhausted the alphabet, and the plot shows where it spent itself. Most of these storms peaked in the Gulf of Mexico or the Caribbean, packed into the left half of the plot. Only four peaked east of 60 degrees, and one of them, Vince, is out near the coast of Portugal at longitude -19, which is a strange place for a hurricane to be.
The crowding on the left is the weakness of this geometry. Katrina and Arlene peaked close enough together that their labels collide, and Jose, Bret, and Stan are piled on top of one another in the Bay of Campeche. Nudging helps, but it cannot untangle labels that genuinely overlap. The honest fix is usually to label fewer things, which is what question 11 does.

Back to a single storm. In the last notebook we plotted Katrina’s wind speed against the day of the year and said that connecting the points was the obvious next thing to want. Do that now with geom_line.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter((c.name == "Katrina") & (c.year == 2005))
    .ggplot(aes(c.doy, c.wind))
    .geom_line()
)










The line geometry takes a color aesthetic just as the point geometry does. Plot wind against day of the year for the four strongest storms of 2005, Dennis, Katrina, Rita, and Wilma, with one colored line each.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .filter(c.name.is_in(["Dennis", "Katrina", "Rita", "Wilma"]))
    .ggplot(aes(c.doy, c.wind))
    .geom_line(aes(color=c.name))
)









Four storms, four lives, spread across three months. Dennis comes and goes in July, Katrina and Rita overlap in the same terrible fortnight at the end of August, and Wilma, the strongest of the four, does not even begin until October.

If a line can connect a storm’s wind speeds in order, it ought to be able to connect its positions in order. Try it: take Katrina again and draw her track, longitude against latitude, with geom_line. Look closely at what comes back and explain what the geometry has done.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter((c.name == "Katrina") & (c.year == 2005))
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_line()
)









Answer: The track has been replaced by a sawtooth. The line geometry does not connect the rows in the order they appear in the data; it connects them in order from left to right along the x-axis. For wind against doy that is the same thing, because the day of the year only ever increases. Longitude does not. Katrina ran west across Florida into the Gulf and then curved back to the northeast, so she visited the same longitudes twice, and the geometry has stitched her early points to her late ones. Reach for a line when the x-axis is time, or something else that only moves one way. A path across a map is not that, which is why last week’s track had to be points.

Bars. Using the peak table from question 5, draw one bar per storm whose length is that storm’s peak wind speed. Put the name on the x-axis and the wind on the y-axis, then add .coord_flip() so the names are readable.



View code
(
    peak
    .ggplot(aes(c.name, c.wind))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)









The bars come out neatly ranked, strongest at the bottom, and the four storms that dominated the season separate themselves from the other seventeen at a glance. Nothing in the plotting code asked for that ranking. Where did it come from?
Sort peak alphabetically and draw exactly the same plot again.


View code
(
    peak
    .sort(c.name)
    .ggplot(aes(c.name, c.wind))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
)









Answer: The bars are drawn in the order the rows appear in the table. The first plot was ranked by wind because peak still carried the sort from question 5, and the second is alphabetical because we just re-sorted it. The geometry has no opinion about which order is right; it takes the one you hand it. So the order of the bars is a real choice you are making, whether or not you realize you are making it, and .sort() is how you make it deliberately. Chapter 7 returns to this with categories whose order depends on a summary of the group itself, such as its count or its median, rather than on a column you can sort directly.

Any geometry can be given its own dataset with the data= argument, which is the standard way to make one part of a plot stand out from the rest. Draw all the 2005 tracks as faint points, then draw Katrina’s track on top of them in "#F5276C" with her name beside her peak. You will need to save Katrina’s rows to a variable first, and you can reuse peak for the label by filtering it.



View code
katrina = (
    storm
    .filter((c.name == "Katrina") & (c.year == 2005))
)
katrina_peak = (
    peak
    .filter(c.name == "Katrina")
)

(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.2)
    .geom_point(color="#F5276C", data=katrina)
    .geom_text(
        aes(label=c.name),
        color="#F5276C",
        nudge_y=2.5,
        size=10,
        data=katrina_peak
    )
)










Every plot so far has been labeled with raw column names, which is fine while you are the only person looking. This one is worth showing to someone else. Take the previous plot and add a .labs() layer giving the axes real names and the plot a title.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point(alpha=0.2)
    .geom_point(color="#F5276C", data=katrina)
    .geom_text(
        aes(label=c.name),
        color="#F5276C",
        nudge_y=2.5,
        size=10,
        data=katrina_peak
    )
    .labs(
        x="Longitude",
        y="Latitude",
        title="The 2005 Atlantic hurricane season",
        subtitle="Katrina's track shown in pink"
    )
)









Nothing about the data changed between the last two blocks. The difference is who the plot is for.

covid = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/france_departement_covid.csv")




Questions
This notebook uses a record of the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic in France. Each row reports the situation in one département (the administrative region France is divided into, of which there are 101) on one date between March and October of 2020. The columns deceased and recovered are running totals, while hospitalised and reanimation are snapshots of how many patients were in the hospital and in intensive care on that day. The two columns ending in _new count new admissions that day.
This is real data, downloaded as it was published, and it has all the type problems the chapter warns about.

import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"




View code
storm = pl.read_csv(ub + "data/storms.csv")




Questions
This notebook uses the record of North Atlantic tropical cyclones kept by the U.S. National Hurricane Center. A row is not a storm. It is one observation of one storm at one moment: where the center of the storm was (lon and lat, in degrees), how fast its winds were blowing (wind, in knots), what Saffir-Simpson category it had reached, and a two-letter status code, where TD is a tropical depression, TS a tropical storm, and HU a hurricane. The remaining status codes describe systems that are not quite tropical. Positions are logged every six hours, so a storm that lasts a week leaves behind about thirty rows. The columns year, month, day, and hour give the time of the observation, and doy gives the day of the year, counting from 1 on the first of January.
Unless a question says otherwise, just print the result of each block; do not save it to a variable.

Make a scatter plot of all 25,112 observations with longitude on the x-axis and latitude on the y-axis.



View code
(
    storm
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
)









Nothing in that code knows what a map is, and yet the outline of one is there. The points fan out from the tropics on the lower left, bunch up over the Gulf and the Caribbean, and drift northeast into the open Atlantic, which is the path storms take. The middle of the plot is a solid black mass, so this is the last plot we can read this way.

There are too many points to follow any single storm. Plot the same two columns again, but only for the 2005 season, which produced 688 observations across 21 named storms.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.year == 2005)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
)










One of those 2005 storms was Katrina. Filter down to the rows where name is "Katrina" and plot the track. The result is not one storm. What happened?



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.name == "Katrina")
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
)









Answer: The filter returns 70 rows describing three different storms. The Hurricane Center recycles names on a six-year rotation, so a name is reused until a storm is bad enough to have its name retired. There was a Katrina in 1981 and another in 1999 before the one in 2005. The name alone does not identify a storm. The name and the year together do.

Fix the previous plot by filtering on the name and the year at once. You should be left with 34 observations.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter((c.name == "Katrina") & (c.year == 2005))
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
)









Now the shape of the storm’s path is clear. Katrina formed near the Bahamas, crossed the southern tip of Florida, turned northwest into the Gulf of Mexico, and came ashore in Louisiana before running up into the Ohio valley.

The plot above shows where Katrina went but says nothing about how strong it was. Using the same two filters, plot the day of the year on the x-axis and the wind speed on the y-axis.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter((c.name == "Katrina") & (c.year == 2005))
    .ggplot(aes(c.doy, c.wind))
    .geom_point()
)









The whole life of the storm took nine days, from day 235 to day 243. It strengthened slowly, crossed Florida, then doubled in strength in about forty-eight hours over the warm water of the Gulf, peaking at 150 knots. The collapse on the right of the plot is landfall. Each point is a separate reading taken six hours after the last one, which is why they are evenly spaced. Drawing a line between them is the obvious next thing to want, and it is the first thing we will do next class.

Allen ran almost the entire length of the basin, from the open Atlantic through the Caribbean and into southern Texas.

Make a scatter plot with category on the x-axis and wind on the y-axis, using every row of the data. What does this plot tell you about hurricanes?



View code
(
    storm
    .ggplot(aes(c.category, c.wind))
    .geom_point()
)









Answer: Nothing. The seven columns of points do not overlap at all, because the category is not a second measurement of the storm. It is calculated from the wind speed by looking up which band the speed falls into: 65 to 80 knots is a category 1, 140 knots and above is a category 5, and anything under 35 knots is recorded as a -1, meaning the system was not yet a tropical storm. A plot of two columns usually tells you how two things relate to each other in the world. Here it tells you the definition of a word. It is worth knowing which of your columns were measured and which were derived from the others, because only the first kind can surprise you.

Since the category is just the wind speed in disguise, it makes a convenient filter. Plot the location of every observation that reached category 5.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter(c.category == 5)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lon, c.lat))
    .geom_point()
)









There are only 136 such observations in seventy years. They are spread across the Caribbean, the Gulf, and the open Atlantic, but they all sit low on the plot: not one of them is north of 30.3 degrees of latitude, which is roughly the level of Jacksonville. Storms this size need very warm water underneath them, and it runs out long before they reach the latitude of New York.

Now look at the season. Plot the day of the year against the wind speed for every row in the dataset.



View code
(
    storm
    .ggplot(aes(c.doy, c.wind))
    .geom_point()
)









The outline of the hurricane season is the upper edge of this cloud. The record starts in early May and runs to the end of December, but almost everything above 100 knots happens between day 220 and day 295, which is mid-August to late October. Notice also that the points fall into rows rather than spreading out smoothly. Wind speed is reported in five-knot steps, so thousands of observations land on the same handful of values and sit exactly on top of one another. Twenty-five thousand points went into this plot and you cannot tell which parts of it are crowded. The tools for fixing that come later.
There is one other thing to see here: a small clump of points off on its own at the far left, before day 20, cut off from the season by three empty months. Find out what those are by filtering the data and taking one row per storm.

(
    storm
    .filter(c.doy < 100)
    .unique(subset=["name", "year"])
    .select(c.name, c.year, c.month, c.day, c.wind, c.status)
)

Two storms, seventy years apart. Alice arrived on New Year’s Day of 1955, and Alex was a genuine January hurricane in 2016. A plot of 25,112 points led us to the two strangest rows in the data, which is a good argument for plotting things before you summarize them.

Do hurricanes weaken as they travel north? Take the observations from 1990 onward where the status was "HU", add a column giving the wind speed in miles per hour instead of knots (multiply by 1.15078), and plot latitude against that new column.



View code
(
    storm
    .filter((c.status == "HU") & (c.year >= 1990))
    .with_columns(wind_mph = c.wind * 1.15078)
    .ggplot(aes(c.lat, c.wind_mph))
    .geom_point()
)









The answer is yes, but the shape is a ceiling rather than a slope. Weak hurricanes turn up at every latitude, so the bottom of the plot stays flat. The top does not. The strongest winds, up around 185 miles per hour, only ever appear between about 12 and 30 degrees, and by 40 degrees nothing in the record has passed 115. Try the plot once more with c.wind in place of c.wind_mph. It is the same picture with different numbers on the axis, which is all that changing a unit should ever do to a graphic.
